statement: What happens after MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD ends is known from the sponsor's phase 2 programme only through two follow-ups without a comparison group. In the first US trial, 16 of the 19 people treated with MDMA were reassessed 17 to 74 months (mean about 45) after their last MDMA session: their mean CAPS score was similar to that 2 months after their second MDMA session (23.7 against 24.6; mean change −0.9 points, 95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, editors' calculation), but individual scores moved widely in both directions; 2 of the 16 scored above the trial's entry threshold again, which the authors count as relapse; 3 of the 19 were not reassessed; and at follow-up 8 of 19 were in psychotherapy and 12 of 19 took psychiatric medicines. On a questionnaire written by the investigators, all 19 reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; 8 reported some cannabis use and 1 psilocybin use, all of whom had used these before the trial, and 1 reported using ecstasy once (Mithoefer et al., 2013). In pooled open-label data from four other phase 2 trials, corrected after an ethical violation by two therapists at one site and under an expression of concern, mean CAPS-IV scores 12 months after treatment were lower than at the end of treatment (35.3 against 42.5 on a 0 to 136 scale; 58 participants), by which time everyone had received full-dose MDMA (Ponte et al., 2021, and its correction, 2025). The sponsor's pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (Jerome et al., 2020) is among the retracted papers described in this section and is not used; the follow-up of the phase 3 trials is the subject of a separate claim in this section. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In one small early trial, 16 of 19 people were checked again about 4 years later. On average their PTSD scores were about the same as soon after treatment, but some people got much better and some much worse, and 2 had moderate-to-severe PTSD again. Many were also getting other therapy or medicines, and there was no comparison group. In four other early trials, scores a year later were a little lower than at the end of treatment, again with no comparison group, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach by two therapists at one site.
population: Adults with chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD treated with MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in the sponsor's phase 2 trials (first US trial, 19 treated with MDMA; four later trials pooled, 59 after the correction)
exposure: Two or three MDMA sessions within manualized psychotherapy (randomized stage or open-label crossover)
comparator: None at follow-up: the same participants' scores at the end of treatment
outcome: PTSD symptom severity (CAPS-IV) 12 months and 17 to 74 months after treatment; relapse (CAPS above 50); later psychotherapy and psychiatric medicines; self-reported benefit, harm and drug use during follow-up
magnitude: First US trial (Mithoefer 2013): CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) 2 months after the second MDMA session and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, n = 16, matched t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; editors' calculation from Table 2: mean change −0.9 (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9), SD of individual changes 31.4, 6 of 16 improved and 3 worsened by 10 points or more; CAPS above 50 in 2 of 16 (13%), or 5 of 19 (26%) counting the 3 not reassessed as negative outcomes; at follow-up 8 of 19 in psychotherapy (16 of 19 at enrolment) and 12 of 19 on psychiatric medicines (12 of 19 at entry). Questionnaire: 19 of 19 some benefit, 0 of 19 harm; cannabis 8, psilocybin 1 (all with earlier use), ecstasy once 1. Four pooled phase 2 trials, corrected (Ponte 2021; correction 2025): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12 months; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008, N = 58.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 1st to 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Original trial: 20 randomized (12 MDMA, 8 placebo with the same psychotherapy); 7 of 8 placebo participants crossed over to open-label MDMA, so 19 were treated with MDMA; follow-up added by protocol amendment; CAPS and IES-R completed by 16 of the 19 (one lost after moving, two declined, one of them having had the smallest earlier response and fearing symptoms would be triggered); CAPS 17 to 74 months after the final MDMA session (mean 45.4, SD 17.3, n = 17).

evidence.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) at 2 months and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), p = 0.72; 2 of 16 completers (13%) above 50 at follow-up, the cut-off for entry to the original study, which the authors call relapse to moderate-to-severe PTSD; counting the 3 non-completers as negative outcomes too, 5 of 19 (26%).

Editors' calculation from the 16 completers' individual scores, which reproduce Table 1's means and SDs: mean change from 2 months to follow-up −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, paired t −0.11), SD of individual changes 31.4; 6 improved by 10 points or more and 3 worsened by 10 points or more (the two relapses from 16 to 60 and from 6 to 91). For the 8 participants who later had a third MDMA session, the 2-month score was taken before it.

evidence.locator: Results › Participation in psychotherapy; Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In psychotherapy at enrolment 16 of 19, at follow-up 8 of 19; on psychiatric medicines 12 of 19 at entry and at follow-up. The authors state there was no meaningful control group at follow-up, that natural history or uncontrolled variables could explain the results, and that later psychotherapy and medicines are the most important confounder and preclude a definite conclusion about long-term benefit.

evidence.locator: Results › LTFU questionnaire results for 19 PTSD subjects › Degree of benefit, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period
evidence.extracted: On the investigators' own follow-up questionnaire, all 19 MDMA-treated participants reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; cannabis use by 8 (once to occasionally) and psilocybin mushrooms by 1, all of whom reported use before enrolment; 1 participant reported using ecstasy once, in an attempt at a therapeutic setting, and found it unsatisfactory.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Footnotes › Conflict of interest
evidence.extracted: The follow-up CAPS was administered in person or by phone by the same independent rater as in the original trial; the sponsor paid this rater, who is the second author, and played a role in the study design, data analysis and writing.

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 3; Summary of corrections made › Open-label endpoints, 1st paragraph (revised text)
evidence.extracted: Corrected open-label analysis of the four pooled trials (N = 58): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12-month follow-up; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008.

evidence.locator: Results › Open-Label Endpoints: Treatment Exit and Long-Term Follow-Up, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 note; Method › Measures › PTSD Symptoms, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: After the blinded endpoint, all participants received full-dose MDMA in open-label sessions; groups were pooled for treatment exit and the 12-month follow-up, which took place after the final open-label session, so these comparisons are within-person and uncontrolled. CAPS-IV total severity scores range from 0 to 136.

Expression of concern (3 December 2024): an ethical violation by a pair of therapists who treated 4 of the 6 MP-4 participants caused a protocol deviation; the authors had not told the journal at submission in December 2019, although the violation was publicly announced in May 2019; the data of those therapists are removed by correction; the journal judged the non-disclosure improper and its investigation of human-subjects ethics inconclusive.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Jerome 2020 row)
evidence.extracted: Across the studies reviewed to October 2023, conclusions were possible only for acute and short-term side effects, because insufficient data were available on longer-term risks beyond active treatment; the one included study that formally assessed long-term follow-up outcomes was the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials by Jerome et al. (2020), which the PMC reference list now marks as retracted.
Among the review's research priorities: longer follow-ups in clinical trials, because short-term outcomes, positive and negative, often change in the weeks and months after a typical trial ends.

risk_of_bias.note: Uncontrolled follow-ups with unblinded outcome assessment (in the first trial by a co-author paid by the sponsor), 16% not reassessed, co-treatment in most participants, an unvalidated questionnaire, and, for the pooled data, an expression of concern and analysis choices made after inspecting outcomes.

imprecision.note: 16 participants in the long follow-up; the 95% interval for the mean change runs from a 17.6-point improvement to a 15.9-point worsening.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down, but the programme's other long follow-up is retracted, so the published record is thin.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about what was observed after treatment in two cohorts without comparison groups (METHODS §6.3: descriptive claims start low). Rated down once for risk of bias (unblinded and partly sponsor-paid assessment, missing data, co-treatment, an unvalidated questionnaire, an expression of concern on the pooled data) and once for imprecision (16 people in the long follow-up, with an interval compatible with large improvement or large worsening). The claim does not say that the benefit lasted because of MDMA: neither follow-up can separate the treatment's effect from later therapy, medicines or the natural course. Both follow-ups come from the same sponsor's phase 2 programme and share investigators, so their agreement is not independent replication.
